issues.name: UCC Article 2 governs; merchant status
issues.rule: Article 2 governs sales of goods; merchant rules apply to those who deal in goods of the kind or hold themselves out as having special knowledge.
keyFacts: old-looking football seemingly autographed by Bart Starr
bought for $100 at a flea market
Mary is a football fan
Dan and Ed are friends
issues.analysis: A football is a good, so the UCC applies. None of the three is a merchant, so no merchant-only rules.

issues.name: Formation of Mary-Dan contract
issues.rule: Contract needs offer, acceptance and consideration; under UCC 2-204 a contract can be made by any manner showing agreement.
keyFacts: Dan offered Mary $10,000 for the ball
Mary wrote 'Dan agrees to buy Mary's Bart Starr football for $10,000 on or before December 1, 2016'
Dan signed
issues.analysis: Dan's offer was accepted by Mary and the napkin states the terms; exchange of goods for price is consideration. A contract exists.

issues.name: Statute of frauds – UCC 2-201
issues.rule: A sale of goods for $500 or more needs a writing indicating a contract, signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought, with quantity.
keyFacts: $10,000 price
napkin signed in pen by Dan but not by Mary
Dan and Ed both signed the assignment/assumption document
issues.analysis: Mary's suit is against Dan and Ed, who both signed (Dan the napkin and the later document, Ed the assumption document), so the statute is satisfied; Mary's lack of signature is irrelevant.

issues.name: Assignment and delegation to Ed; liability of Dan and Ed
issues.rule: A contract can generally be assigned and duties delegated unless performance is personal or prohibited (UCC 2-210); the delegating party remains liable unless the obligee agrees to a novation; a promisor who assumes duties is liable to the obligee as an intended third-party beneficiary, and an assignee takes subject to defenses against the assignor.
keyFacts: Dan hereby assigns all of his rights to buy Mary's football to Ed; Ed hereby assumes all of Dan's obligations
signed by Dan and Ed, one copy sent to Mary
payment of money is not personal
issues.analysis: Valid assignment of Dan's right and delegation of payment duty to Ed; Ed is bound to Mary by assumption and Dan stays liable since Mary never released him. Mary can sue both.

issues.name: Breach – failure to pay by December 1
issues.rule: Buyer's failure to pay on time is a breach; payment and delivery are concurrent conditions, and the seller must show ability and willingness to tender. Lack of funds is no excuse.
keyFacts: Dan was unable to come up with $10,000
Mary sued on December 2, 2016
Dan and Ed no longer wanted the ball
issues.analysis: Neither Dan nor Ed paid by December 1, so there is breach absent a valid defense; Mary must show she was ready to tender the ball.

issues.name: Defense – mutual mistake
issues.rule: A contract is voidable by a party who was mistaken, along with the other party, about a basic assumption on which the contract was made that materially affects the exchange, unless the party seeking avoidance bears the risk of the mistake (conscious ignorance or allocation by the agreement).
keyFacts: Mary and Dan both assumed it was a genuine autographed game ball used in 1967 Super Bowl
signature genuine but ball was a consumer product made after 2005
ball worth about $1,000 not $10,000
Mary bought it for $100 at a flea market; 'old-looking' and 'seemingly autographed'
issues.analysis: Both parties shared a mistake on a basic assumption that made the deal ten times over its value, which favors rescission. Mary will argue Dan bore the risk (nothing warranted, sold as is/ 'seemingly') and conscious uncertainty; Ed, as assignee, takes subject to Dan's defense and shared the same mistake. A close call but likely rescission.

issues.name: Other defenses – frustration of purpose / misrepresentation / warranty
issues.rule: Frustration excuses a party where a supervening event destroys the principal purpose; the doctrine fits poorly with a mistake that existed at formation. Innocent misrepresentation or a description warranty (2-313) could also be raised.
keyFacts: napkin only says 'Bart Starr football'
Mary only assumed the ball's history
issues.analysis: Frustration is an imperfect fit (the mistake pre-dated the contract); no misrepresentation or warranty by Mary as to the game-ball status. Mutual mistake is the proper defense.

issues.name: Damages – seller's remedy and from whom
issues.rule: Seller's damages for buyer's repudiation: contract price minus market price at time and place for tender (2-708(1)) or resale (2-706), plus incidental damages less expenses saved; action for the price only when goods cannot reasonably be resold (2-709); duty to mitigate. Dan and Ed are both liable.
keyFacts: contract price $10,000
ball is worth about $1,000
Dan stays liable absent novation; Ed assumed the obligation
issues.analysis: Mary would recover about $9,000 (price less $1,000 value) plus incidentals from Dan and Ed jointly, not the full $10,000 and not specific performance of the sale; if mistake succeeds she recovers nothing (perhaps restoration).

notes: Answer A states damages as the full $10,000 and Answer B only from Ed; correct measure is price minus market and both Dan and Ed. Mutual-mistake outcome (risk allocation) is a close call.

issues.name: Larceny – the cash
issues.rule: Larceny is trespassory taking and carrying away of personal property of another with intent to permanently deprive.
keyFacts: Donna reached into the car and grabbed the purse
removed the cash from the wallet
threw the purse back into the car
issues.analysis: Donna took and kept the cash without consent, intending to deprive permanently. Larceny of the cash is clear (except for the police-decoy consent issue).

issues.name: Larceny – the purse (no intent to permanently deprive)
issues.rule: Intent to permanently deprive is required; discarding or returning the item shows no such intent for the item itself.
keyFacts: Donna threw the purse back into the car
issues.analysis: Donna did not intend to keep the purse, so no larceny of the purse; only the cash is larceny.

issues.name: Police decoy – consent and trespass; attempt
issues.rule: If the owner or police consent to the taking, the taking is not trespassory and larceny fails, though attempt remains (factual impossibility is no defense).
keyFacts: Donna and Alice were not aware that the purse had been placed in the car by police officers as part of an undercover crime investigation
Officer Oscar observed everything
issues.analysis: Placement by police may negate trespass (consent), so possible only attempted larceny; most courts treat a decoy offering mere opportunity as not consent. Close call.

issues.name: Burglary / robbery
issues.rule: Common-law burglary requires breaking and entry of a dwelling of another at night with intent to commit a felony; modern statutes cover other structures; robbery requires taking from person or presence by force or fear.
keyFacts: a parked car with its windows down
Donna reached into the car
no person present or force
issues.analysis: A car is not a dwelling or structure under most statutes, no breaking, and no force or fear, so no burglary or robbery (some statutes cover vehicles).

issues.name: Solicitation of Alice
issues.rule: Solicitation is asking or encouraging another to commit a crime with intent that the crime be committed; it merges into the completed offense or conspiracy.
keyFacts: Donna said 'I want you to go to the corner and shout to me if you see a police officer coming'
Alice is twelve
issues.analysis: Donna asked Alice to act as lookout for the larceny, intending the crime; solicitation is complete on asking. Merges if convicted of conspiracy or larceny.

issues.name: Conspiracy (Donna and Alice)
issues.rule: Conspiracy is agreement between two or more persons to commit an unlawful act with intent, plus an overt act in some jurisdictions; MPC uses unilateral approach, common law requires two guilty minds.
keyFacts: Alice said 'Look, Mom, there is a purse on the seat'
Alice walked to the corner and kept looking for police
Donna grabbed the purse
issues.analysis: Implied agreement by conduct (Alice went to the corner), overt act by taking; but if Alice, a child, lacks capacity there may be no bilateral agreement; MPC unilateral approach would still reach Donna. Close call.

issues.name: Donna's defense – entrapment
issues.rule: Entrapment: government inducement to commit a crime the defendant was not predisposed to commit; mere opportunity is not inducement.
keyFacts: purse left on seat by police of an undercover investigation
Officer Oscar only observed
issues.analysis: Police merely provided an opportunity and Donna acted readily (enlisting a lookout), showing predisposition; entrapment fails.

issues.name: Alice – accomplice liability (lookout)
issues.rule: An accomplice aids, abets or encourages with intent that the crime be committed; a lookout aids.
keyFacts: Alice kept looking for police
she did not shout because no police appeared
Alice pointed out the purse
issues.analysis: Alice served as lookout with apparent knowledge and intent, so accomplice to larceny of the cash; assistance need not succeed in the act (no warning was needed). Intent depends on what she understood.

issues.name: Alice – conspiracy and solicitation
issues.rule: Alice's remark about the purse is not a solicitation; any conspiracy depends on her agreement and capacity.
keyFacts: 'Look, Mom, there is a purse on the seat of that car'
issues.analysis: Mere observation is not solicitation; conspiracy is arguable by implied agreement but weak given her age.

issues.name: Alice's defense – infancy
issues.rule: At common law a child aged 7 to 14 is presumptively incapable of crime but the presumption can be rebutted by showing understanding of wrongfulness (Cal. Penal Code 26: clear proof).
keyFacts: Alice is twelve-year-old
pointed out the purse and walked away to watch for police at mother's request
issues.analysis: Rebuttable presumption: the state would argue she understood the wrongfulness from her pointing out the purse and keeping watch, but she acted at her mother's direction; arguable either way.

issues.name: Alice's other defenses – entrapment, parental coercion
issues.rule: Entrapment as above; duress requires threat; acting at a parent's direction is not itself a defense but bears on capacity.
keyFacts: Alice acted at her mother's request
undercover police purse
issues.analysis: Entrapment fails as to Alice as with Donna; no duress facts.

notes: Neither answer discussed the police-decoy consent issue (trespass vs attempt). Check burglary conclusion for vehicles under modern statutes; B concluded burglary may be satisfied, which is doubtful.

issues.name: Arson – malice
issues.rule: Common-law arson is the malicious burning of the dwelling of another; malice is intent to burn or reckless disregard of an obvious risk of fire.
keyFacts: lit several firecrackers in his yard, and threw them at Heather's house
he wanted to wake her up to discuss
tools filled with gasoline stored in the wooden toolshed
Two of the firecrackers landed in the toolshed, setting it afire
issues.analysis: Throwing lit firecrackers at a house with a wooden shed holding gasoline equipment shows reckless disregard of an obvious risk of fire, even though Tom only wanted to wake Heather; malice is likely (he used the hose, a mitigating fact).

issues.name: Arson – dwelling or structure of another
issues.rule: Common law required a dwelling (including attached outbuildings/curtilage) of another; modern statutes cover any structure.
keyFacts: wooden toolshed abutted Heather's house
Tom lives next door and does not own it
issues.analysis: The shed abuts the house and falls within the curtilage/dwelling or modern structure definition, and it belongs to Heather, so the element is met.

issues.name: Arson – 'burning' requirement
issues.rule: Some actual burning (charring) of the structure is required; smoke or soot damage alone is insufficient, but any charring suffices.
keyFacts: The inside of the toolshed suffered smoke damage
all items inside destroyed
Tom extinguished the fire before it spread
fire set the wooden shed afire
issues.analysis: Key factual question: the shed was set afire, but only smoke damage is described and the contents (not the structure) were destroyed. If no charring of the structure, no arson; a wooden shed fire probably charred it, a close call.

issues.name: Attempted arson and lesser offenses
issues.rule: Attempt requires specific intent to commit the crime and a substantial step; alternative statutes punish reckless burning or malicious mischief.
keyFacts: wanted to wake her up to discuss what he had seen
firecrackers thrown at a wooden house
Tom put out the fire
issues.analysis: Attempt requires intent to burn, which Tom lacked (only wished to wake Heather), so attempted arson is weak; reckless burning or malicious mischief for the destroyed tools may fit better.

issues.name: Defense – voluntary intoxication
issues.rule: Voluntary intoxication negates only specific intent; it is no defense to malice/recklessness crimes (arson is general intent or malice).
keyFacts: took three pills, then four more, though box said no more than two every eight hours
never used Anxiety-Fix before
fell asleep, woke from nightmare
issues.analysis: Tom's overdose was voluntary and arson requires only malice (reckless disregard), so intoxication is no defense (possibly relevant to attempt specific intent). He also acted purposefully, which undercuts incapacity.

issues.name: Defense – involuntary intoxication
issues.rule: Intoxication is involuntary if the substance is taken without knowledge of its intoxicating effect or under coercion; exceeding the dose is not involuntary, but unexpected effects of an unfamiliar medication may qualify.
keyFacts: Anxiety-Fix is over-the-counter
never used before
instructions stated maximum two pills
issues.analysis: Tom ignored label directions, so the intoxication is voluntary; involuntary-intoxication argument based on unfamiliar drug is weak.

issues.name: Defense – diminished capacity / emotional distress
issues.rule: Most jurisdictions limit mental-state defenses to insanity or specific-intent mens rea evidence; emotional upset is not a defense to a malice crime.
keyFacts: saw Heather kissing another man
felt queasy
nightmare about Heather
issues.analysis: Emotional distress and anxiety do not excuse arson; diminished capacity is generally unavailable for a general-intent/malice offense.

issues.name: Heather – arson of her own dwelling for insurance
issues.rule: Common law allowed owners to burn their own property, but modern statutes criminalize burning one's own property with intent to defraud an insurer; arson requires a burning caused by the defendant.
keyFacts: Heather had been having a hard time selling her house
her insurance would cover the loss
squirted flammable fluid on the windowsills of the house
issues.analysis: No burning of the house resulted from Heather's act (the fire was put out), so completed arson of the house fails; shed damage was caused by Tom.

issues.name: Heather – attempted arson
issues.rule: Attempt requires specific intent and an act beyond mere preparation (substantial step); abandonment is not shown.
keyFacts: grabbed a can of lighter fluid
opened windows near the shed
squirted fluid on the windowsills
Tom extinguished the shed fire
issues.analysis: Heather intended the house to burn and spread accelerant to the house next to a burning shed, a substantial step beyond preparation; attempted arson is likely, with fraud intent supporting modern statutes.

issues.name: Heather – attempted insurance fraud / false pretenses
issues.rule: Attempted fraud requires specific intent to defraud and a step beyond preparation; burning the house to collect would be remote from filing a claim.
keyFacts: insurance would cover the loss
issues.analysis: No claim was filed and the act of burning is preparation, so attempted false pretenses is too remote.

issues.name: Heather – malicious mischief
issues.rule: Malicious mischief is malicious destruction of the property of another.
keyFacts: Heather's lighter fluid on windowsills
tools in the shed destroyed by Tom's fire
tools used by Tom; shed is Heather's
issues.analysis: Heather did not destroy the shed or tools (fire did) and sprayed her own windowsills, so charge is weak.

issues.name: Heather – accomplice or conspiracy with Tom
issues.rule: Accomplice liability requires aid or encouragement with intent that the principal commit the crime; no agreement here.
keyFacts: Heather acted after Tom's fire
Tom and Heather unaware of each other's actions
issues.analysis: Heather did not assist Tom's act or share intent about his fire; accomplice liability does not fit.

notes: Burning/charring question is fact-dependent; reviewer should check this. Both answers' treatment of Heather's malicious mischief (A,B) is weak; Answer B treats tools as Tom's but tools are likely Heather's.

issues.name: Betty – battery (intent and harmful/offensive contact)
issues.rule: Battery is an intentional act causing harmful or offensive contact with another; intent means purpose or substantial certainty of contact.
keyFacts: Albert pushed her in order to get past her
Betty fell and hit her head, suffering a debilitating brain injury
issues.analysis: Albert intended the push (contact), so intent is met even though he did not intend the brain injury; battery is clear.

issues.name: Betty – causation and scope (slippery floor, unforeseen injury)
issues.rule: In intentional torts the defendant is liable for all harm proximately caused, including unforeseen consequences of the contact; the injury need not be intended.
keyFacts: Albert dropped the watermelon making the floor slippery
Betty slipped on the spilled watermelon
hit her head
issues.analysis: The fall was a natural result of pushing someone on a slick floor Albert created; Albert liable for full brain injury.

issues.name: Betty – defenses (provocation)
issues.rule: Verbal provocation is not a defense to battery; self-defense requires threat of force.
keyFacts: Betty loudly criticized him as 'clumsy'
Albert was humiliated
issues.analysis: Humiliation or insult does not privilege Albert's push; may only bear on punitive damages.

issues.name: Betty – damages
issues.rule: Compensatory damages (medical expenses, lost earnings and earning capacity, pain and suffering); punitive damages for malice or conscious disregard; nominal not needed.
keyFacts: debilitating brain injury
Albert pushed to get past her
issues.analysis: Large compensatory award; punitive damages possible but less likely because the push was impulsive rather than aimed at injury.

issues.name: Carl – assault
issues.rule: Assault is an intentional act creating reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact.
keyFacts: pushed it violently at Carl
Carl jumped out of the way
The cart missed Carl
issues.analysis: Violently pushing a cart at Carl with intent to cause apprehension; Carl's dodge shows awareness. Assault established (miss is irrelevant).

issues.name: Carl – damages
issues.rule: Assault damages are for emotional distress/apprehension; nominal damages available without actual harm; punitive damages possible.
keyFacts: Carl was not hurt
issues.analysis: No physical injury, so nominal and perhaps emotional distress damages; punitive possible given violence.

issues.name: Duane – battery by transferred intent
issues.rule: Intent to commit assault or battery on one person transfers to an unintended victim for battery.
keyFacts: The cart missed Carl, but struck Duane, an elderly shopper, on his back side
Albert intended to put Carl in apprehension
issues.analysis: Albert's intent to assault Carl transfers to the battery of Duane, who need not have been aware of the contact.

issues.name: Duane – eggshell plaintiff and damages
issues.rule: Defendant takes the plaintiff as he finds him and is liable for the full extent of harm, even if enhanced by a pre-existing condition; compensatory plus possible punitive.
keyFacts: Duane, who had an unstable heart condition, suffered a heart attack as a result
elderly shopper
issues.analysis: Albert is liable for the heart attack even though unforeseeable; medical costs, pain and suffering and other compensatory damages; punitive less likely.

issues.name: Edna – trespass to chattels (mistake of owner)
issues.rule: Trespass to chattels is intentional interference with another's chattel causing damage; intent to do the act suffices, mistake about ownership is no defense (transferred intent from Betty's car).
keyFacts: used his car key to leave a deep gouge in the finish on all four sides of the car
he believed was Betty's
car belonged to Edna
issues.analysis: Albert intended to damage the car, so mistake as to owner is no defense; trespass to chattels established.

issues.name: Edna – conversion alternative
issues.rule: Conversion is an intentional interference so serious that the defendant must pay full value; extensive but repairable damage typically stays trespass.
keyFacts: gouges on all four sides
issues.analysis: Damage is likely trespass to chattels (repair cost), not conversion unless it makes the car worthless.

issues.name: Edna – damages
issues.rule: Repair cost or diminution in value, loss of use, plus punitive damages if malicious.
keyFacts: deep gouge on all four sides
finish damaged
issues.analysis: Edna recovers repair cost (or diminution) and loss of use; punitive damages possible because act was deliberate vandalism, although Albert targeted Betty's car.

notes: Answer A states Duane died, which is not in the facts. Reviewer may check whether punitive damages for transferred-intent victims is covered.
